name: U-Net semantic segmentation of Sentinel-2 patches

identity.method_name: U-Net (encoder-decoder CNN with skip connections), custom-trained 4-class semantic segmentation of Sentinel-2 patches
identity.core_idea: U-Net is a convolutional encoder-decoder network with skip connections between mirrored down- and up-sampling stages, originally designed for biomedical image segmentation and now the default architecture for pixel-wise land-cover mapping. Here it would be trained from scratch on the project's own Sentinel-2 patches to assign every pixel to one of four classes: open water, water hyacinth/macrophyte, bare lake bed, or built-up. Unlike A2 (pretrained water-only CNNs) and A3 (SAM, class-agnostic), this is the only one of the three that could natively output the exact 4-class scheme the project needs, but only if it is trained on locally-produced labels.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. No official dataset ID exists for this exact 4-class scheme. The project would build its own training set from COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED-equivalent Earth Search STAC L2A scenes (bands B02, B03, B04, B08, B11, SCL) over MGRS tile 43PGQ; no GEE/Kaggle catalog product matches 'open water / hyacinth / bare bed / built-up' as a single labelled product.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Programmatic weak supervision, stacked with manual correction. Seed labels: MNDWI > 0 for a first-pass 'open water' class and NDVI > 0.30 for a first-pass 'vegetation' class (the project's own current-method thresholds), then manually split the NDVI-positive pixels inside the lake polygon into 'hyacinth/macrophyte' versus normal shoreline vegetation by eye on true-colour composites, and manually delineate 'bare lake bed' (exposed dry mud/silt) versus 'built-up' (permanent structures) using the same composites plus OpenStreetMap building footprints as a weak prior. Cost: this is genuinely free of a purchased label set but is not free of effort -- it is the single largest cost driver in this item (see student_days). It is not fully unsupervised and not transfer-from-a-labelled-dataset, because no external dataset carries this exact 4-class scheme.
fit_to_project.input_required: Multi-band Sentinel-2 image patches at the project's fixed 20 m EPSG:32643 grid, using the six cached bands (B02, B03, B04, B08, B11, SCL); SCL would be used for cloud/shadow masking rather than as a classifier input feature. The project already has the imagery. What it does NOT have and must build: pixel-level or patch-level class masks for all four classes, per lake-year.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed. Training operates per-pixel or per-patch, not per-lake-year. Reframing 42 lake-year scenes at ~900,000 pixels/scene gives a nominal ~37.8 million pixel-labels, but this number is misleading: pixels inside a single lake-year are strongly spatially autocorrelated (adjacent pixels share class almost by construction), so the true number of independent training signals is far smaller and is bounded above all by the number of physically distinct lake shorelines and hyacinth mats present, not raw pixel count. For a defensible held-out test, the only clean unit remains the lake (6 clusters) or the lake-year (42), because any pixel- or patch-level split leaks: a random pixel split puts neighbouring pixels of the same lake into both train and test. Practically: usable independent patches per lake-year, at a 64x64-pixel (1.28 km) patch size, range from roughly 1 patch for the smallest lake (Sankey Tank, ~12.4 ha, about 310 total 20 m pixels, i.e. smaller than one patch) up to a few dozen for Bellandur (~315 ha footprint). Effective sample size for cross-lake generalisation testing is therefore n=6 (spatial blocks), not 42 and certainly not 37.8 million.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels. Source: MNDWI/NDVI threshold rule (already computed by the current baseline) plus manual visual delineation per lake-year for the hyacinth/bare-bed/built-up split, cross-checked for Bellandur and Varthur against Bareuther et al. 2020 (MDPI Remote Sensing, doi 10.3390/rs12223843), which independently mapped macrophyte vs algae vs free water for exactly those two lakes 2002-2019 using supervised maximum-likelihood classification (not deep learning, but a genuine external cross-check for 2 of the 6 lakes). Estimated labelling effort: 5-8 student-days for careful polygon delineation across 42 scenes using QGIS, assuming the water/vegetation split is seeded automatically and only the hyacinth/bare-bed/built-up refinement is manual.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Yes, workable, because the model is trained from scratch directly on the project's own 20 m grid rather than inheriting a fixed resolution assumption from someone else's pretrained weights (contrast with A2's Landsat-30 m-trained DeepWaterMap or A3's SAM, trained on arbitrary-resolution natural photographs). The real constraint is not resolution mismatch but absolute pixel count: Sankey Tank's ~310 total pixels at 20 m leaves too few pixels per class to give any patch-based sampling scheme a stable per-class count, and U-Net's successive 2x downsampling stages (typically 4-5 levels) can exceed the spatial extent of the smallest lakes, forcing a shallower network or smaller patch size than a textbook U-Net.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: Weak/proxy labels: MNDWI/NDVI thresholds (automated) plus manual visual delineation for hyacinth, bare bed, and built-up classes, cross-checked against Bareuther et al. 2020 for Bellandur/Varthur only.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Partially addresses (3) no real ground truth, by forcing an explicit, documented, falsifiable weak-label procedure to stand in place of encroachment labels -- but it does not eliminate the fundamental absence of a legal ground truth, since the weak labels are still self-generated and only checked against a single external classical-classification paper for 2 of 6 lakes. Does not fix (1) the 42-row constraint at the final reporting level: whatever pixel-level accuracy is achieved, the risk/trend conclusions the project reports are still rolled up to 42 lake-year rows. Does not touch (2) the static OpenStreetMap-buildings problem. Does not touch (4) one dry-season scene per year; the model still only ever sees the same single annual scene the project already has.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: Not automatically, but it is the one item of the three genuinely positioned to help, if the 'bare lake bed' class is well-calibrated. A single-date 4-class classifier cannot by itself know that a bare patch is 'drained for desilting' rather than 'filled in by encroachment' -- that distinction is temporal and contextual, not visible in one scene. However, having a dedicated bare-lake-bed class (distinct from built-up) creates the raw material for a follow-on rule: a lake-year that shows bare-bed-not-built-up followed by a return to open water is consistent with desilting, while bare-bed-then-built-up is consistent with encroachment. The U-Net itself only supplies the per-year class map; the disambiguation logic has to be added on top, most naturally by a change-detection or time-series rule (see A4/A9/C9 in the wider study) applied to the U-Net's own multi-year outputs.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: Yes, directly, and this is the item's central selling point: a dedicated 'water hyacinth/macrophyte' class, separate from 'open water,' is exactly the mechanism the current MNDWI/NDVI baseline lacks (hyacinth registers as vegetation under NDVI, not water under MNDWI, which is precisely the Bellandur 2019 confound: 16 ha water vs 260 ha vegetation inside a 315 ha footprint). If the hyacinth class is reliably labelled and learned, this method resolves the confound in principle. The main open risk is that the weak/manual labels used to train that class are themselves uncertain, so the model's separation quality is only as good as the labelling effort behind it.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None on its own. The model's output is a land-cover class raster, not a legal boundary; it still only overlays whatever boundary is chosen elsewhere in the project (OpenStreetMap multipolygon by default, or a Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority / Bhuvan / National Wetland Atlas boundary if item B2 substitutes one in). At the project's fixed 20 m grid, a 30 m Bengaluru Master Plan buffer (the currently reinstated figure per the Supreme Court ruling) is only 1-2 pixels wide, so even a perfect land-cover classification cannot meaningfully resolve encroachment specifically inside that buffer -- this is a grid-resolution problem the model cannot fix, only inherit.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Genuinely year-varying for all four classes, because each year's scene is classified independently -- this is a real strength relative to the project's static OpenStreetMap building counts (limitation 2). The caveat is that each year still contributes only one classification (the single dry-season scene the project has), so within-year seasonal variation (e.g. hyacinth bloom timing) is invisible regardless of how good the classifier is.

implementation.libraries: PyTorch with segmentation-models-pytorch (smp, BSD-3 license) for a U-Net decoder over a small ResNet/EfficientNet encoder, or a compact from-scratch U-Net in Keras/TensorFlow; rasterio and geopandas for raster/vector I/O; albumentations for patch augmentation; scikit-learn for confusion-matrix/F1 reporting.
implementation.pretrained_weights: No off-the-shelf pretrained weights exist for this exact 4-class scheme. The encoder backbone can optionally be initialised from ImageNet weights (trained on 3-channel RGB, 224x224 natural photographs), but the project's input is 5-6 bands including SWIR -- adapting a 3-channel pretrained first layer to 5-6 channels (by replicating or zero-padding extra channels) is standard practice but dilutes the value of the pretrained weights, and ImageNet features were never trained on Sentinel-2 spectral response curves. Training the whole network from scratch on this small dataset is equally plausible given how little data volume is actually involved.
implementation.licence: Fully open for the project's own use: segmentation-models-pytorch is BSD-3-Clause, PyTorch is BSD-style, all code would be student-authored. No third-party weight or data licence risk, since no external pretrained checkpoint specific to this task is being reused.
implementation.compute_requirement: CPU-feasible in principle given the tiny data volume (42 scenes x ~900,000 pixels x 6 bands, well under a few hundred MB as float32), but a small GPU materially speeds up training; free Colab/Kaggle T4 GPU sessions comfortably cover training a compact U-Net on this dataset in well under an hour per run, with many runs needed for the leave-one-lake-out cross-validation loop (6 folds) and hyperparameter iteration. Reproducible end to end by a solo student with no lab cluster.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 10-16 student-days honestly, broken down as: 5-8 days for weak-label seeding plus manual correction of the hyacinth/bare-bed/built-up classes across 42 scenes; 3-5 days for model build, leave-one-lake-out training loop, and hyperparameter/patch-size tuning (small lakes need a smaller patch size than a textbook U-Net); 2-3 days for evaluation, visual QA, and writeup. This is the most labour-intensive of the three A-group items because it is the only one that requires building a genuinely new labelled dataset.

evaluation.metrics: Per-class F1 and IoU across the four classes (mean IoU / macro-F1), plus a full confusion matrix. Accuracy alone is not adequate: built-up and bare-lake-bed pixels are a small minority of most lake polygons, so a trivial classifier that always predicts 'open water' or 'hyacinth' can score high raw accuracy while being useless for the two classes the project actually needs (bare bed for the desilting confound, built-up for encroachment itself). A secondary, arguably more decision-relevant metric is the derived per-lake-year water-area and hyacinth-area estimate compared against the current MNDWI/NDVI baseline, since that is the number that ultimately feeds the 42-row table.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Leave-one-lake-out is the only defensible primary split: train on pixels/patches from 5 lakes, test on the 6th, repeated 6 times, because pixels within a lake-year are massively spatially autocorrelated (adjacent pixels of the same lake share vegetation type, shoreline development pattern, and imaging conditions almost by construction). Leave-one-year-out (train 2019-2023, test 2024-2025) is a useful secondary check for temporal generalisation but is a weaker basis given only 7 years. A naive random k-fold split on pixels or patches drawn from only 6 underlying lakes will leak lake identity into the test fold and must not be used, exactly as the project's own leakage warning states for the 42-row tabular data.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Two concrete leakage paths: (1) spatial autocorrelation -- any pixel- or small-patch-level random split puts near-duplicate neighbouring pixels of the same lake shoreline into both train and test, inflating apparent accuracy without testing generalisation to a new lake; (2) label circularity -- because the water and vegetation seed labels come from the exact MNDWI/NDVI thresholds the model is meant to be compared against, evaluating the model only on agreement with those same thresholds would just measure how well it reproduces the seed rule, not whether it is actually better. Independent manual spot-checks (and the Bareuther 2020 cross-check for Bellandur/Varthur) are required to break this circularity.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None natively. A plain U-Net produces a bare per-pixel softmax score, which is not a calibrated probability. To defend any interval at the panel, this would need Monte Carlo dropout, a small deep ensemble (e.g. 5 models from different leave-one-lake-out folds), or a conformal-prediction wrapper (item C7 in the wider study) applied to the per-pixel or per-lake-year class-area outputs. Given the project has zero ground truth and only 42 rows, presenting a bare point estimate with no interval is hard to defend and should be treated as a known gap, not an oversight.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Low risk for standard geometric/photometric patch augmentation (flips, rotations, brightness/contrast jitter) used to multiply the small patch count -- this is safe, standard practice and does not fabricate a trend. The risk becomes real only if temporal or class-balance augmentation is used to synthesise plausible-but-unobserved states (e.g. interpolating a 'hyacinth' mask for a year that was not actually labelled, or oversampling minority-class pixels using a generative method) -- if that is done, it must be disclosed explicitly, since it could manufacture an apparent encroachment or hyacinth trend that was never actually observed in the source imagery.

evidence.published_performance: General Sentinel-2 water-body U-Net-family studies report strong open-water-only accuracy: NDR U-Net (Nested Dense Residual U-Net, IIETA Revue d'Intelligence Artificielle, doi 10.18280/ria.380324) reports test-set IoU 93.27%, test accuracy 95.60%, test precision 90.88%, test recall 86.90% on 5,682 Sentinel-2 images over Europe (confirmed directly from the primary source). AER U-Net (attention-enhanced multi-scale residual U-Net, Scientific Reports 2025, s41598-025-99322-z) reports improved water-body segmentation over baseline U-Net variants [verify -- full-text metrics table was behind an authentication redirect and could not be independently confirmed in this session]. None of the located studies use the project's exact 4-class scheme (open water / hyacinth / bare bed / built-up); all located quantitative U-Net results are for binary open-water-vs-not-water segmentation, which is a materially easier task than the 4-class problem this item proposes.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: NDR U-Net: Europe, 5,682 Sentinel-2 images, temperate rivers/lakes, no hyacinth or seasonal desilting analogue. AER U-Net: general benchmark water-body datasets [verify region, not confirmed]. Neither is a tropical, hyacinth-infested, seasonally-drained urban lake setting, so neither number is a direct forecast for 6 Bengaluru lakes.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No published deep-learning (U-Net or otherwise) study was located that applies this exact 4-class scheme to Bengaluru or other Indian urban lakes. The closest domestic precedent is Bareuther, Klinge & Buerkert (2020), 'Spatio-temporal dynamics of algae and macrophyte cover in urban lakes: A remote sensing analysis of Bellandur and Varthur wetlands in Bengaluru, India,' Remote Sensing 12(22):3843, doi 10.3390/rs12223843 -- which solves the macrophyte/algae/free-water separation problem for exactly 2 of the project's 6 lakes, but with supervised maximum-likelihood classification (a classical method), not a CNN. This weakens, rather than strengthens, the case that a U-Net is strictly necessary: the paper shows the class-separation problem the project cares about was already solved with a simpler classifier over a comparable domain.
evidence.evidence_recency: Strongest generic U-Net-for-water evidence is 2023-2025 (Scientific Reports 2025, IIETA 2023-2024 window). The only India/Bengaluru-lake-specific evidence (Bareuther et al.) is 2020 and pre-dates the deep-learning approach entirely, and is itself analysing imagery only through 2019.
evidence.primary_sources: NDR U-Net: https://doi.org/10.18280/ria.380324 (IIETA, Revue d'Intelligence Artificielle). AER U-Net: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-99322-z (Scientific Reports, 2025) [verify -- full text not directly accessible this session]. Bareuther, Klinge & Buerkert (2020): https://doi.org/10.3390/rs12223843 (MDPI Remote Sensing 12(22):3843). Xu 2006 MNDWI reference (current baseline, for comparison): H. Xu, 'Modification of normalised difference water index (NDWI) to enhance open water features in remotely sensed imagery,' International Journal of Remote Sensing, 2006. Earth Search STAC (imagery source): https://earth-search.aws.element84.com/v1.

risk.failure_modes: With only 5-8 student-days of weak/manual labelling, the hyacinth and bare-lake-bed classes inside the smallest lakes (Sankey Tank, ~310 total 20 m pixels) will have too few labelled pixels for any per-class statistic to be stable; 20 m mixed pixels at the exact shoreline (where encroachment would actually show) are inherently a blend of water and vegetation signal, causing systematic error precisely where the project needs precision; if the seed thresholds (MNDWI/NDVI) dominate the training signal, the model risks simply re-learning the current baseline rule, which would not constitute an improvement worth reporting as a new deep-learning contribution; leave-one-lake-out testing collapses to only 6 folds, so any reported metric will carry very high fold-to-fold variance that must be reported honestly (e.g. mean +/- range across the 6 folds), not as a single number.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask directly: 'where did the hyacinth, bare-bed, and built-up labels come from, since no ground truth exists?' The honest answer -- a mix of index thresholds and manual visual delineation, cross-checked against one external paper for 2 of 6 lakes -- is defensible if disclosed plainly and if the manual step is described as a documented, repeatable procedure rather than ad hoc judgement, but it is indefensible if presented as though it were independent ground truth. The panel will also ask how a per-pixel land-cover map becomes a legally meaningful encroachment number; the honest answer is that it does not, on its own -- it requires the separate geo-fencing/buffer layer (items B1/B2) as a second step, and at 20 m resolution that buffer is only 1-2 pixels wide.
risk.honest_expectation: Realistically achievable here: a working 4-class pixel classifier that visibly separates hyacinth from open water more cleanly than the current fixed-threshold MNDWI/NDVI baseline, and that supplies a genuinely useful bare-lake-bed signal as raw material for a desilting-vs-encroachment rule built on top of it. This is a real, reportable, useful improvement over the null baseline on the land-cover-mask question. It will NOT, by itself, resolve the project's core problems: it does not manufacture legal ground truth, does not change the 42-row sample size at the reporting level, and does not by itself distinguish desilting from encroachment (it only supplies one necessary ingredient for that distinction). A null or mixed result on the headline 'did we detect encroachment' question is likely and should be reported as such if it occurs; a positive result on 'is this a better land-cover mask than MNDWI/NDVI' is plausible and worth reporting either way.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time -- this is the guide's explicit 'one deep learning model' requirement and the most internally consistent option of the three A-group items, since it trains end-to-end on the project's own 20 m, 6-band data with no incompatible pretrained-weight or resolution assumption to inherit, and it is the only one of the three that can natively produce the hyacinth-separating 4-class output the project needs. The condition is that the weak-label procedure and its cost (5-8 student-days) must be budgeted honestly and disclosed plainly, and the leave-one-lake-out (n=6) variance must be reported rather than hidden behind a single headline number.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We trained a small 4-class U-Net directly on our own Sentinel-2 patches to separate water hyacinth from open water and to flag bare lake bed, which the current MNDWI/NDVI rule cannot do, using weak threshold-plus-manual labels because no encroachment ground truth exists; it improves the land-cover mask over the baseline but does not, by itself, prove encroachment.
